title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. Using a curated multi‑intent 300‑task manifest, a frozen deterministic validator encoding syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic reachability and destructive‑pattern checks, and the declared model snapshot gpt-5-mini, every shared initial candidate passed the validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300; n11=300, n10=n01=n00=0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10k resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred the preregistered guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked. We publish all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest, the preregistration, and analysis artifacts (hash‑signed) to support reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for operator‑intent→vendor‑CLI translation in NetOps. Practical adoption demands operational safeguards (deterministic validators, bounded repair policies, audited artifacts). Generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) is a common architecture intended to improve safety by rejecting or repairing harmful or invalid initial generation before deployment. Prior work has explored intent translation, LLM‑assisted configuration, and verification techniques (see Related Work). However, the marginal safety benefit of adding a bounded deterministic repair step to a fixed initial generation has not been robustly quantified under an artifact‑archived, preregistered paired design.

We asked the preregistered research question: to what extent does a deterministic, bounded G‑V‑R pipeline increase the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation? Our core contribution is an artifact‑anchored, preregistered paired experiment (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6) that (1) uses a curated 300‑task manifest, (2) freezes one shared initial generation per task (shared‑initial design), (3) compares baseline (validator(initial)) vs guarded (validator(initial) OR validator(repair) with a single automatic repair), and (4) publishes every raw response, provider trace, and deterministic scoring trace with canonical hashes. All run artifacts and analysis are archived and hash‑signed (execution_manifest and specific artifact hashes appear in Table 2).
sections.related_work: Relevant prior work divides into (A) LLM‑assisted intent→configuration systems and intent‑based networking (Nguyen et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., CNSM 2024; Mondal et al., 2025), (B) deterministic/formal network verification (Bagpipe/SMT approaches, Weitz et al., 2016), and (C) G‑V‑R and tool‑assisted self‑correction work in NLP and agent systems (INTERACSPARQL style self‑refinement and LATCH‑style bounded lookahead). Benchmarks and validator design choices (NetLLMBench, UniAIOps) motivated our conservative validator construction. We verified cited sources and include verified record identifiers in the Cited Record Ids list for provenance; all cited items referenced in this paper correspond to archived evidence records in the run bundle.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered a paired binary design on n=300 tasks. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the per‑task probability difference that the guarded arm yields a validator pass vs the baseline arm). The preregistration fully specifies inclusion/exclusion rules, retry policy, contamination detection, analysis tests (exact two‑sided McNemar and paired bootstrap percentile CI), multiplicity handling (single primary test), and the single‑repair bounded policy. The frozen preregistration SHA‑256 is given above.

Task manifest. We used a curated 300‑task multi‑intent manifest limited to vendor CLI fragments (intent, initial and expected final state, per‑task workflow policies, and difficulty metadata). The canonical manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Each entry encodes intent text, initial network state, required safe command sequences, and policy constraints (examples: "must_be_down_for_fields" and make‑before‑break patterns). Representative tasks (000001–000006) are included in the evidence bundle and below.

Validator. Scoring used a conservative deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0). The validator performs: (1) vendor‑specific CLI parsing and canonicalization; (2) syntactic validation; (3) enforcement of per‑task workflow invariants (e.g., must‑be‑down rules, make‑before‑break, minimum active interfaces); (4) detection of destructive patterns (global shutdowns, uplink disable); and (5) generation of structured validator traces (final_state, parsed_command_count, violation_codes). Validator traces are archived per episode (execution/scoring/*.json). The validator intentionally omits dynamic/emulation‑level routing checks to remain fully deterministic and reproducible in the published container.

Model, prompt, and execution contract. The declared model snapshot was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Execution used a single shared initial generation per task (one model call per task) to isolate the marginal effect of repair on a fixed initial candidate (shared‑initial design). Provider calls and raw responses are archived (execution/provider_calls/*, execution/responses/*). The run budget allowed at most one repair call per task in the guarded arm; the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 600. The run used deterministic seeds logged in the execution manifest.

Confirmatory analysis. The primary test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test on paired binary outcomes, with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) predeclared. Sensitivity analyses for contamination and missingness are specified: contaminated pairs would be flagged and treated in predeclared sensitivity variants; missingness policies (failed calls) were logged and handled per preregistration. All analysis code and outputs are archived (analysis/*).

sections.discussion:
Interpretation of ceiling outcome. The observed ceiling (300/300 initial validator passes) implies that under the declared model snapshot, prompt, and curated manifest the single shared initial generation already satisfied the conservative deterministic validator for every task. Because the guarded arm can change outcomes only when that shared initial candidate fails, the guarded single‑repair policy could not be exercised. The paired difference 0.00 with p=1.00 and collapsed CI [0.00,0.00] is therefore a valid, degenerate but informative experimental outcome under the preregistered design.

Why the result is useful. Although null in the sense of no measured repair benefit, the run delivers operationally relevant evidence: (1) it quantifies a case where the generator+prompt produced robust, validator‑passing candidates across a diverse curated task set, (2) it shows the bounded cost of adding the guarded policy would have been nonzero (additional orchestration and model calls) but produced no benefit in this configuration, and (3) the fully archived artifacts permit replication and controlled variants (harder tasks, independent draws, iterative repair budgets, richer validators) that alter the estimand and test operational regimes where G‑V‑R might help.

Design consequences and limits. The preregistered shared‑initial‑candidate design intentionally isolates the repair benefit for a fixed initial draw: both arms use the identical initial generation per task so the guarded arm's only potential to improve the binary outcome is by successfully repairing an initial failure. This design reduces between‑generation variance noise but creates the possibility of a ceiling effect: if the single initial draw by the generator is valid for most tasks (as here), the repair branch cannot demonstrate benefit. This tradeoff was predeclared in the preregistration and is discussed in the Limitations section. If one wishes to measure expected population gains from repeated generation draws, an alternative design (independent per‑arm initial draws or repeated generations) should be used; the archived manifest and scripts support those variants.

Vendor heterogeneity and manifest provenance. The task manifest contains per‑task metadata and adapter annotations including vendor/adapter labels (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) and per‑task difficulty tags; the canonical manifest is archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a7...). The run bundle does not include a precomputed in‑paper vendor count table as a numeric summary artifact; the manifest encodes vendor labels so readers can compute exact per‑vendor counts from the archived manifest programmatically. We therefore provide the manifest path and canonical SHA so independent verification is straightforward; we did not invent or fabricate per‑vendor counts in the paper text because the artifact is the authoritative source. Representative response files embed vendor‑specific CLI tokens; these are available in execution/responses/* for quick inspection. If reviewers require an explicit numeric per‑vendor breakdown presented in the PDF, we will compute the counts exactly from the archived manifest and add the computed, hash‑referenced table in a revision, but we must not invent counts not present in the archived artifacts.

Threats to validity. Internal: shared‑initial design (ceiling effect risk), single model snapshot and prompt, deterministic validator scope. Construct: deterministic validator covers syntactic and workflow invariants but omits full dynamic routing/emulation checks—validator passes do not guarantee absence of deeper runtime failures. External: single model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and curated manifest limit generality; additional models, randomized draws, adversarial tasks, or richer validators may yield different conclusions. Conclusion validity: paired sample size is adequate for the preregistered estimand under the planned sensitivity assumptions, but zero discordant pairs collapses inferential variance (CI collapsed to a point) and limits information about repair effectiveness. The full preregistration and execution logs list these threats and provide scripts to rerun variants.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation of a bounded G‑V‑R policy across a curated 300‑task manifest. Under the declared generator/prompt/model and a conservative deterministic validator every shared initial LLM candidate passed (300/300), so the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no measurable improvement (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This ceiling result is informative: it demonstrates one realistic regime where a carefully prompted generator produces validator‑passing outputs across a diverse set of tasks and where the added orchestration cost of a bounded repair policy did not yield benefit. The evidence bundle publishes all raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, the curated task manifest, preregistration, and analysis artifacts with canonical hashes to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator depth, model family, and repair budgets. We recommend future studies examine independent per‑arm draws, iterative repair strategies, and validators that include dynamic or emulation checks to evaluate operational safety beyond deterministic syntactic/workflow invariants.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, destructive‑pattern detection) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
